episodes.213286: Warm temperatures during early April began to melt 2-3 feet of dense snowpack that had fallen across parts of northern Michigan in the historic mid-March winter storm, including Beaver Island. Several rounds of heavy rainfall occurred across northern Michigan through mid-April as well, resulting in total rainfall through the month of April across northern Michigan ranging from 5 to as much as nearly 16 inches at the Wellston Tippy Dam cooperative observing site in southeastern Manistee county. Traverse City, Houghton Lake, and Gaylord all recorded their wettest Aprils on record. Coupled with thawing ground and saturated soils, this resulted in widespread historic flooding across all of the northern Lower Peninsula. 20 USGS river gauges in the region set new all-time records, most of which broke the previous records by 1-2 feet. This, too, resulted in enhanced concern for multiple high-impact dams to be overtopped, including the Cheboygan Dam in the town of Cheboygan, which reached a height of just under 6 inches from the top at its peak, and the Bellaire Dam in northwest Lower Michigan. Many inland lake levels further upstream in the Cheboygan River basin were also well above normal, resulting in damage from flooding and ice shoves as winds pushed chunks of floating ice into homes along the shores; the high groundwater content and high water levels also caused widespread impacts to public and private water supplies and wastewater treatment facilities. Multiple portions of multiple roads also failed during this period, including M-119, the Tunnel of Trees, a famous tourist route along the Lake Michigan coastline between Harbor Springs and Cross Village, and the heavily-trafficked Beitner Rd Bridge south of Traverse City on the Boardman River; the river gauge at this latter location was also swept away when the culverts and roadway failed. Portions of roads that received damage are likely to remain closed for months. The Pellston Regional Airport, KPLN, was closed from April 11 until May 5th due to significant flooding over the runways; the airport did not return to full operations for both runways until June 1. By April 15th, Michigan governor Gretchen Whitmer had declared a state of emergency for 21 counties in northern Michigan within the WFO Gaylord, MI forecast area; President Donald Trump issued a Major Disaster Declaration for these same counties on June 30th. Total flood damage estimates as of July 2026 exceeded $800 million.

events.narrative: Significant amounts of snowmelt on still-frozen ground, coupled with multiple rounds of heavy rainfall resulting in 4-7 inches of rainfall across the entirety of the county, resulted in significant and widespread flooding in Cheboygan County. Emergency management put out a statement by mid-month that all roads in Cheboygan county had some portion covered in water, with not enough road closed signs to go around; the sheriff's office stated nearly every waterway in the county have overflowed beyond their banks, swallowing docks, roads, yards, and in far too many cases, homes. Homes and businesses along the Sturgeon River near Wolverine were damaged by flooding, and around 200 homes in Indian River were damaged by flooding, with one homeowner reporting his refrigerator was definitely floating at one point. The three largest inland lakes across the Tip of the Mitt region -- Burt, Mullett, and Black Lakes -- all had high water levels with damage resulting to surrounding homes and roads due to flooding. The high water levels, coupled with strong winds, allowed for an ice shove, where lingering lake ice piled up into many homes on the downwind side of the lake, causing further damage beyond flooding alone. The Cheboygan Dam, a significant-risk dam 1.5 miles from the outlet of the Cheboygan River (the outlet for all lakes/rivers in Cheboygan county) and 0.75 miles from downtown Cheboygan and US-23, was under intense scrutiny for concerns of being overtopped due to the significant amounts of water in the basin, and the US-23 bascule bridge in Cheboygan was raised on April 13 due to debris concerns; this stayed up for several days, resulting in detoured traffic and economic impacts to businesses in the community. Dams further upstream in the basin, including the Alverno and Kleber Dams on the Black River, were also scrutinized and repaired as needed to keep water from surging downstream into the Cheboygan Dam, and a hydroelectric power generation plant at the Cheboygan Dam complex was quickly repaired and restarted to further aid in increasing flows through the dam. The dam's highest peak was just over 6 inches from the top. A levee on the Little Black River north of Cheboygan was breached on the 14th, unrelated to the Cheboygan Dam concerns, and resulted in evacuations on the north edge of the city of Cheboygan. Flooding continued into mid-May.

Warm weather following the historic 2-3ft wet, dense snowfall from the Mid-March Winter Storm led to snowmelt, and over the course of the month, an additional 5-7 inches of rainfall fell across the county, resulting in significant and widespread flooding; a state of emergency for Emmet county was declared by the 15th, and flooding impacts across the county continued into the month of May. The Pellston Regional Airport, KPLN, was closed from April 11 until May 5th due to significant flooding over the runways; the airport did not return to full operations for both runways until June 1. Two portions of M-119, the Tunnel of Trees along the coastline of Lake Michigan between Harbor Springs and Cross Village, were closed due to washouts:  the stretch from Terpening Rd to West Stutsmanville Rd was closed due to a significant washout on the steep slopes near the road, leaving the roadway compromised and closed through at least summer. South of Cross Village, a culvert was overwhelmed, causing the roadway to fail completely, and will also remain closed for much of the summer. Significant flooding impacts were noted in Pellston, Petoskey, Alanson, Cross Village, and the Crooked River Locks.

Significant, widespread flooding occurred across Antrim county due to snowmelt and 6-12 inches of rainfall through the course of the month, most of which fell in a few days in the middle of the month. This resulted in damage to businesses, homes, and roadways, with significant home foundation damage estimates as high as $50,000 to $100,000 per house. Some erosion under a berm along the Bellaire Dam was noticed on the 13th, resulting in emergency repairs and monitoring as water levels behind the dam reached the highest peak in its recorded 100 year history:  lake levels on Intermediate Lake, upstream from the Bellaire Dam, rose from 8.61ft on the 11th to 10.38ft on the morning of the 14th, and a discharge rate of 90,000 gallons per minute through the dam was not enough to lower river levels during the peak of the flooding. Water came within 12 inches of overtopping the dam...with additional concerns over a culvert upstream near Ellsworth. Residents of much of the town of Bellaire were put on alert from the 13th through the 19th for potential evacuations as a result.

Widespread flooding throughout the county by mid-month, following a couple rounds of heavy rainfall and continued snowmelt from the mid-March winter storm; up to 6-10 inches of rainfall occurred during the month. Waterways were swollen due to the overabundance of water combined with frost still in the ground. Flooded roads were first noted on the county emergency management's social media page on the 13th, and a state of emergency was declared by the county on the 14th with portions of multiple roads in the county fully closed to roadway failures and water over roads.

Significant, widespread flooding due to snowmelt and a monthly total of 7-15 inches of rain across the county, resulted in an emergency declaration for the county. The culverts for the Boardman River beneath Beitner Rd, a major road carrying 20-40,000 vehicles per day south of Traverse City, were overwhelmed on the evening of the 14th, resulting in total bridge failure in a matter of a few minutes; the USGS river gauge at this site was also swept away. Downstream, at the former Union St. Dam/new FishPass site, the river came within a half inch of meeting the 500-year flood level. Multiple roads and bridges around Traverse City and elsewhere within the county were periodically closed, either due to failures/sinkholes or to reassess roadway conditions following heavy rains. Evacuations occurred throughout the county, including the Kingsley and Mayfield areas, and 8 people were rescued by boat near Mayfield, with several floating propane tanks also secured for safety purposes. Damage estimates in Grand Traverse county alone exceeded $15 million, after only 20 percent of road and infrastructure assessments completed by mid-May. No known injuries or fatalities due to flooding were reported as of mid-May.

A state of emergency for Benzie county was declared on the 14th of April, following multiple rounds of heavy rainfall that resulted in high water levels at the significant-risk Homestead Dam on the Betsie River, upstream from US-31; 1200 sandbags were quickly placed in order to stop ongoing erosion on dam embankments which kept the dam from failing. A monthly total of 8-12 inches of rainfall was recorded across the county, with additional impacts to roads and property countywide due to flooding.

Flooding impacts began around the 12th, with road closures due to shoulder failures and complete culvert and roadway failures beginning around the 14th along the Manistee River, including North Highbridge Rd near the Manistee River. Flooding impacted the Northern Michigan Dragway in Kaleva, delaying its season opener from April 18 to the 25th due to flooding of the track. The Tippy Dam near Wellston on the Manistee River saw high flows; the cooperative observing site at this location recorded a total of 15.68 inches of liquid precipitation for the month of April, with almost half of this falling between the 12th and 15th. This was nearly 3 times the previous highest rainfall for the month of April at this location -- 6.60in in 1929, and the highest monthly total out of all months on record for this location. Consistent records began in 1927.

Significant flooding impacts were noted in the Cadillac, MI area, where 10-15 inches of rainfall countywide through the first half of the month resulted in lake levels on Lakes Cadillac and Mitchell rising 2 ft during the month, peaking on the 19th; the previous lake level record, set in 2008, was broken by 6 inches on the 13th and an additional 5-6in rise was noted the following day. This resulted in damage to even first floors of homes, property, and roadways, with standing water still present in some areas well into June. The wastewater treatment facilities for the city of Cadillac were also impacted by the flooding, with high water levels diminishing effectiveness of sewer lift pumps:  the sanitary sewage depth levels at the lift station at Division and Leeson St. were 20-25ft deep, compared to a normal 4-5ft depth. A state of emergency was declared for the city of Cadillac on the 15th. Some city parks began to open by the 22nd, though high water levels remained. Elsewhere in the county, the Hodenpyl Dam near Mesick on the Manistee River also required some preventative reinforcement on the 16th; the river was up to the base of the M-37 bridge deck over the Manistee River near Sherman, and there was concern about closing multiple Manistee River crossing sites, which would have severely impacted north-south travel across the county.

Significant flooding impacts across Presque Isle county in northeast Lower Michigan, including the eastern section of Black Lake that is within Presque Isle county, resulting in a state of emergency declaration. Several main roads took severe washout damage, including M-68 near Ocqueoc Falls, where a temporary repair was completed by early summer to limp the area through until a full repair could be done in October, causing significant issues for Presque Isle road commission project logistics and planning. Heythaler Highway near Rogers City also suffered severe roadway failure. As of mid June, the Michigan DOT estimate for repairs for the northern Michigan region was at least $6.6 million. The Rogers City wastewater treatment plant, designed to handle 1 million gallons of wastewater per day, was overrun with over twice that on average during the mid-month heavy rains, placing the plant in jeopardy of failure, and residents of the city were asked to reduce water use for this reason.

Flooding impacts were noted on the AuSable river downstream from the Mio Dam in Oscoda county, including at the Foote Dam near Oscoda Wurtsmith Airport, all the way to Lake Huron. Lake levels on Van Etten Lake near Oscoda were also high, and the associated dam was overtopped on the 15th, resulting in flooding near the town of Oscoda.

Significant flooding across the county, particularly on the AuGres and Rifle Rivers. Log jams were removed on April 16 near US-23 and State Rd to stabilize bridge integrity at that location.  On April 17, the water was up to the base of the bridge deck at the AGSM4 river gauge site on the AuGres River near AuGres with the gauge reading 12.06ft...following a new record crest of 12.31ft set the previous day. The crest of 11.64ft on the Rifle River at Sterling was the 6th highest crest on record for that gauge location.

Bucks Pond Dam upstream of Hubbard Lake, northwest of Barton City, failed on the 13th, washing out the associated roadway. Additional reports and video of culvert failures across the county, including near Hubbard Lake and McGregor Rd off M-72.

Significant widespread flooding across the county with high flows on the AuSable River through multiple dams, including the Mio Dam, which was in condition C for high flows from approximately April 12 to April 21. Homes and businesses were damaged by floodwaters. The AuSable River at Red Oak gauge recorded a new record crest of 8.88ft on April 13, which is 2ft higher than the previous record.

Widespread flooding across the county, particularly along the AuSable River, though flooding impacts were noted elsewhere, including in the city of Grayling where some parking lots, roads, and streets were flooded.

The Hillman Dam on the Thunder Bay River in Hillman, MI was overtopped, with water flowing over the right embankment on the 13th; a contractor built a 2-ft berm to shift flow back toward the spillway and the dam returned to normal operating range by the 16th. The Hiawatha-area dams northeast of Atlanta were overtopped, resulting in damage to all three dams in the chain, including roadway damage. A private dam at Becks Red Lantern Campground in Atlanta failed on the 10th, resulting in flooding at the campground.
The Rifle River Recreation Area near Lupton in Ogemaw county was flooded, resulting in the park's closure on the 14th, with water over the bridge at Peters Rd.
Water over roads across Chippewa county, including 6 Mile Rd. at Soo Line Railroad south of Sault Ste Marie, MI, and near Pickford, MI.
Flooding in the county, including in the lower basement of buildings and restaurants in Glen Arbor, including the Mill.

Flooding across the area, including downtown Kalkaska. Rugg Pond Dam, a high-hazard dam on the Rapid River, developed erosion on the embankment on the 7th, resulting in emergency repairs through mid-month.
Widespread flooding impacts across the county, including some full road closures and culvert washouts, water over roads, and flooding of public and private homes and businesses and campgrounds.
Flooding impacts, particularly across the northern portion of the county through which the Manistee River flows.
Reports of flooding on Bois Blanc Island due to heavy rain and snowmelt.
Flooding issues noted across the county, including impacts to main roads. One lane of McCoy Rd at M-32 was closed due to water over the roadway.
Naguabo Emergency Manager reported that Rio Blanco is out of its banks. The Intersection of PR-191 and PR-31, near the highway exit, was closed due to impassibility.

Emergency managers reported flooding affecting PR-956 and PR-186 in Sector Galateo Barrio Bartolo due to the Rio Grande overflowing its banks. The roads are impassable, and local officials have proceeded to close them to the public.

Heavy rain developed over the eastern slopes of Maui.  Emergency management and the local news reported multiple impacts. Hawaii News Now reported Hana High & Elementary School was temporarily closed on Tuesday April 7 due to flooding. The Department of Education said some classrooms had water damage. Water was also reported on Hana Highway.
